ai_show_review.summary: High‑energy early Dead set with scorching Cardboard Cowboy and tight jams
ai_show_review.blurb: The July 29 1966 Vancouver show delivers a blistering first set that includes a definitive Cardboard Cowboy, a crisp Baby Blue, and a smoking Cream Puff War. Garcia’s tone shines, Pigpen’s organ rips, and the band rides a high‑energy groove from start to finish. All three soundboard sources are excellent, making this an essential early‑Dead recording.
ai_show_review.review: July 29, 1966 at the P.N.E. Garden Auditorium captures the Grateful Dead in their embryonic, electrified stride. From the opening “Standing On The Corner” through a seamless run of folk‑rock staples, the band builds momentum that erupts on “Cardboard Cowboy,” where Jerry’s guitar tone is described as perfect and Pigpen’s organ cranks up to full psychedelic thrust. Highlights continue with an immaculate rendition of “It’s All Over Now Baby Blue,” where Garcia’s lead work glides effortlessly, and a smoking “Cream Puff War” that showcases the group’s early improvisational instincts. The set closes on a gritty “Viola Lee Blues,” driven by Phil’s vocal harmonies and a thunderous rhythm section anchored by Bill Kreutzmann. Across three pristine soundboard captures—each praised for crystal‑clear balance and minimal hiss—the performance stands out as a vivid snapshot of the Dead’s 1966 energy, making it a must‑listen for any early‑period collector.

best_recording.reason: Excellent soundboard with crystal‑clear balance, showcasing Garcia’s guitar and Pigpen’s organ without filler tracks.

key_highlights: Scorching Cardboard Cowboy highlights Garcia’s flawless tone and tight band interplay.
Pigpen’s ripping organ drives the set, especially on Viola Lee Blues and Baby Blue.
Cream Puff War delivers a smoking early jam that epitomizes 1966 Dead energy.
Seamless transitions keep the momentum high throughout the entire first set.
song_highlights: It's All Over Now Baby Blue

band_performance.Jerry: Garcia’s tone is consistently praised, especially on “Baby Blue,” “Next Time You See Me,” and the fiery “Cardboard Cowboy.”
band_performance.Phil: Phil adds strong vocal harmonies on “Viola Lee Blues” and provides a solid bass foundation throughout the set.
band_performance.Bob: Bob’s rhythm guitar sits low in the mix but contributes steady support to the band’s drive.
band_performance.Pigpen: Pigpen’s organ is described as ripping, cranked, and a key driver of the early psychedelic sound on multiple songs.
band_performance.Billy: Bill Kreutzmann’s drumming holds the groove together with a tight, propulsive feel that fuels the high‑energy performance.
